paras: The threatened lynching of "Shorty" and "Reddy" took place at McKeesport, Pennsylvania, in August 1881, when a crowd gathered around the borough jail and threatened to lynch two men held as suspected leaders of the gang that had killed merchant George A. McClure. No attack on the jail was reported, and a later item said the two men jailed at McKeesport had no connection with the gang and would be released. The episode reached papers from Maine to Georgia as part of national wire coverage of the McKeesport manhunt.

McClure, a McKeesport hardware merchant, was shot dead while trying to recover stolen goods from a band of thieves, and a constable named Fleming was wounded. According to a Morgantown account, the thieves had gathered near a place called Deadman's Hollow, where McClure, Fleming and a man named Lynch went to watch them. The borough councils offered a $1,000 reward, and the Lancaster Intelligencer reported that if the murderers were found "lynch law will settle them."

Talk of lynching continued through the manhunt. A Pittsburgh dispatch of August 5 described threats at McKeesport that suspects "will not get to Pittsburgh alive," and fifty mounted men were reported to have left the town in pursuit with "a strong determination to lynch them if caught."

A Pittsburg telegram dated August 7 reported that constables had arrested two men near Deadman's Hollow who gave their names as "Shorty" and "Reddy" and were thought to be the gang's leaders. "Shorty" was said to have begged that his mother not be told of the arrest and to have admitted he was the man mentioned in the papers, though he would say nothing more. An "immense crowd" then gathered around the jail, threatening to lynch the men as soon as their identity as the killers was settled. No paper reported an attempt on the jail.

An Ohio weekly reported that the two men jailed at McKeesport on Monday "bear a striking resemblance to two of the party, but have in fact no connection with the bandits," and would be discharged at once. On August 10 two other men, "Shorty" O'Connor and "Reddy" Vasey, surrendered at Hollidaysburg as members of the gang; they were later given a hearing at McKeesport and discharged when nothing connected them to the crime. The coverage does not say whether these were the same men held at McKeesport on August 7.

Only white papers covered the episode, and almost entirely through short wire items. The Washington Evening Star printed the fullest version under the headline "TWO ARRESTS—THREATS OF LYNCHING," whose telegram called doubts about the arrest "folly" and predicted the prisoners might by morning "have graced a lamp post or a tree." The Portland Daily Press and the Daily Kennebec Journal ran two-sentence items on August 9, and the Savannah Morning News included the story in its news summary the next day. None of these reports gave the race of the prisoners or the crowd, and none condemned the threats.
The date of the arrest varies: the Evening Star's telegram and the Portland paper place it on Sunday, August 7, while the Ohio item says the men were jailed on Monday.

No one was killed: the coverage reports only a crowd at the jail threatening lynching, and A11 says the two men held there were to be discharged (A5, A7, A11). The crowd's size is not given beyond 'immense' (A5).

framing.detail: The Evening Star's telegram treated a lynching as likely ('their lives are hardly worth a burying at this writing') and dismissed doubts about the arrest as 'folly', without condemning the crowd.
